o: Marbles occupy positions; each step teleports every marble at moveFrom[i] to moveTo[i] (guaranteed non-empty). Only occupancy matters, never marble counts, so a set of occupied positions suffices: remove moveFrom[i], add moveTo[i], then output sorted. Example 2 shows merges: [1,1,3,3] with moves 1→2, 3→2 collapses to just {2}.
k: Multiplicity is irrelevant — model occupancy as a set.
Each move is two O(1) set operations; sorting happens once at the end.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear Scan with Membership Checks
a.i: Keep occupied positions in a sorted list; for each move, remove the source (guaranteed present) and insert the destination, deduplicating at the end. Straightforward but insertion/removal costs O(L) per move.
s: Build a sorted list of distinct starting positions.
For each (f, t): remove f from the list, insert t.
a.t: O((n + q) log L + L log L) — balanced-tree/set operations per move plus final sort

a.i: Same idea with an unordered hash set: O(1) average per move, then one sort at the end. This is the optimal practical choice.
s: Put all starting positions in a hash set.
For each move, delete moveFrom[i] and add moveTo[i].
Sort the set's contents and return.
a.t: O(n + q + L log L) — O(1) average per move, sorting only at the end

w: Lead with the observation that counts don't matter — that collapses the whole problem to set maintenance. Pitfall: using remove on a Python list inside the loop is O(L) per move and can TLE conceptually at 1e5 scale; prefer sets. Follow-up: track marble counts per position (use a Counter/dict instead of a set).
